newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico rebel leader Marcos takes a public walk.
newsitem.headline: Mexico rebel leader Marcos takes a public walk.
newsitem.dateline: SAN CRISTOBAL DE LAS CASAS, Mexico 1996-11-07

text.p: Zapatista rebel leader Subcommander Marcos emerged from hiding on Thursday and walked around this colonial Mexican city to mark the formation of a peace commission.

Wearing a ski mask and surrounded by supporters and Mexican Red Cross members in a security cordon, Marcos and 15 indigenous leaders of the Zapatista rebels strolled up and down a six-block stretch in the centre of the city to the surprised gazes of onlookers, witnesses said.

Marcos, who is usually found at a rebel camp deep in the Lacandon Jungle, was in San Cristobal for the formal establishment on Thursday of a Follow-up and Verification Commission charged with making sure peace accords reached by the rebels and government are honoured.

Establishment of the commission had been a key condition of the mostly indigenous Zapatistas for resuming full peace talks with the government of President Ernesto Zedillo, suspended by the rebels September 2.
Zapatista commander David, a Tzotzil Maya Indian, called the establishment of the commission "a bridge seeking to establish peace, not war".

The commission was established two days late because of last minute haggling over its make-up. No date was set for a resumption of full talks, although mediators hope they can be restarted next month.
The rebels are also demanding a new government negotiating team and release of Zapatista prisoners as well as implementation of an accord already reached on indigenous rights.
Marcos, the Zapatista chief spokesman and military leader, made no statement to reporters as he wandered about, puffing on his trademark pipe.
At his arm walked Amalia Solorzano, the widow of late ex-President and revolutionary General Lazaro Cardenas, whose son Cuauhtemoc Cardenas leads the opposition Democratic Revolution Party.
Some street vendors in the main square of San Cristobal greeted Marcos with cries of "Viva Marcos!" (long live Marcos) and "Zapatista power!"
The Zapatistas rose up in arms on New Year's Day 1994 to demand greater democracy, indigenous rights and land reform.
At least 145 people died in the early days of the rebellion but there has been almost no fighting since and peace talks have dragged on for more than 18 months.
The commission will consist of academics and politicians designated by the federal and Chiapas state government, the rebels, mediators and civic groups.
